job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup our legal team wants a complete list of the bill's loopholes, ambiguities, and drafting problems: anything that would let us keep operating if it passes as written, or that we can point to as making it unworkable. Can you go through the bill text below and find every one?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Below is a text-only issue inventory, not a conclusion that any particular operation would be lawful. **The strongest apparent openings are the existing-license and environmental-assessment exceptions; most threshold-based openings remain subject to § 2(1)(B)’s discretionary catchall.** Other applicable laws and license conditions could independently restrict operations.

### Definitions and scope

1. **§ 2(1)(A)—Per-vessel rather than aggregate threshold.** The definition measures recovery “by a single vessel,” not by an operator, project, fleet, or affiliated group. Splitting production among vessels could keep each below the threshold, although § 2(1)(B) could reach that activity.

2. **§ 2(1)(A)—Exactly 10,000 metric tons is outside the numerical definition.** “More than 10,000” excludes recovery of exactly that amount or less per vessel per year. This is an apparent quantitative safe zone only under subparagraph (A), not necessarily under the catchall.

3. **§ 2(1)(A)—The annual measurement period is unspecified.** “Per year” could mean a calendar year, rolling 12-month period, or operating year, with no rule for partial years. The choice affects allowable recovery and when a violation begins.

4. **§§ 2(1)(A), 5—Unclear treatment of the threshold-crossing year.** The text does not say whether exceeding 10,000 tons makes earlier recovery that year unlawful retroactively or only triggers liability prospectively. This uncertainty directly affects the potentially substantial daily penalties.

5. **§ 2(1)(A)—No tonnage measurement methodology.** The bill does not specify wet versus dry weight, inclusion of sediment or water, or whether tonnage measures recovered material or contained minerals. Different methodologies could materially change whether a vessel crosses the threshold.

6. **§ 2(1)(A)—“Recovery” and vessel attribution are undefined.** It is unclear whether recovery occurs at seabed extraction, lifting, onboard receipt, or subsequent processing, and which vessel receives the tonnage attribution in a multi-vessel system. Seabed equipment and separate collection, lifting, and transport platforms make this consequential.

7. **§ 2(1)(A)—Depth boundary and measurement uncertainty.** Recovery at exactly 200 meters or shallower is outside subparagraph (A). The bill supplies no depth datum or rule for sites spanning the boundary, though subparagraph (B) could still apply.

8. **§ 2(1)(A)—Resource coverage is broad but undefined.** “Other mineral resources” does not specify whether it includes dissolved minerals, subsurface deposits, or mineral-bearing sediments. “From the seabed” also leaves uncertainty about previously removed material and resources recovered from the water column.

9. **§ 2(1)—“Commercial” does not require a commercial purpose.** Despite the defined term’s label, subparagraph (A) turns on recovery volume, depth, and vessel attribution, not sales, profit, or commercial intent. Noncommercial research could therefore qualify unless an exception applies.

10. **§ 2(1)(B)—The deciding “Secretary” is unidentified.** The bill never defines “Secretary,” while § 6 expressly identifies the Secretary of State. This creates uncertainty about which official may expand the prohibition through risk determinations.

11. **§ 2(1)(B)—No procedure or timing for risk determinations.** The text does not specify rulemaking, individualized orders, notice, publication, or when a determination becomes binding. Operators cannot reliably identify the catchall’s scope in advance, especially where criminal liability is possible.

12. **§ 2(1)(B)—“Comparable” ecosystem risks lack a defined benchmark.** Subparagraph (A) covers activities with potentially very different scale, techniques, and environmental effects. The bill supplies no comparison methodology, probability threshold, geographic scale, or definition of “deep-sea ecosystems.”

13. **§ 2(1)(B)—The catchall is not expressly limited to mining.** “Any activity” could encompass exploration, research, or other ocean uses with comparable risks, regardless of recovery volume or commercial purpose. That breadth creates notice and delegation concerns, although it does not automatically make the provision invalid.

14. **§ 2(2)—The U.S.-person definition omits numerous entity types.** It expressly includes citizens and state-organized corporations, but not LLCs, partnerships, trusts, unincorporated associations, or permanent residents. Those omissions create apparent gaps for activity outside the United States, subject to interpretation and other liability rules.

15. **§ 2(2)—Non-state incorporation is not addressed.** Corporations organized solely under federal, District of Columbia, territorial, tribal, or foreign law are not expressly included. U.S. ownership or control alone does not bring a foreign corporation within the stated definition.

16. **§ 3(a)—“In the United States” lacks a geographic definition.** The bill does not specify its treatment of territories, territorial waters, the exclusive economic zone, the continental shelf, or U.S.-flagged vessels abroad. Existing jurisdictional law may resolve some questions, but the text leaves important offshore boundaries uncertain.

17. **§ 3(a)—Indirect participation is not expressly delineated.** “Engage in” does not specify the treatment of financing, contracting, equipment supply, transportation, processing, or purchasing recovered minerals. Some conduct could constitute participation or incur liability under other law, but the bill does not clearly define that boundary.

### Exceptions

18. **§ 3(b)—No specified issuer or jurisdiction for qualifying exploration licenses.** The exception does not identify a licensing statute, agency, country, or international authority. Its literal wording could encompass pre-enactment exploration licenses issued by multiple authorities.

19. **§ 3(b)—Potential mismatch between exploration licenses and commercial mining.** The exception exempts “mining conducted under an exploration license” without a bill-specific production cap. Whether commercial-scale recovery qualifies depends on what “under” means and what the underlying license actually authorizes; the exception does not itself enlarge that authorization.

20. **§ 3(b)—No express restriction on amendments, renewals, or transfers.** The bill does not explain whether an old license retains exempt status after renewal, expansion, transfer, or changes in operator. Nor does it freeze exempt operations to their pre-enactment footprint or methods.

21. **§ 3(b)—“Existing operations” need not actually be operating.** The operative language requires a pre-enactment license, not commencement of mining before enactment. A dormant qualifying license could therefore support later activity if its terms permit it.

22. **§ 3(b)—No environmental conditions on grandfathered activity.** The exception contains no independent risk limit, assessment requirement, or termination mechanism. Because it disapplies § 3(a), the catchall definition does not appear to override an otherwise qualifying exception.

23. **§ 3(c)—Environmental-assessment purpose is undefined.** There is no limitation on recovery volume, duration, methods, sale of recovered material, or commercial sponsorship. Substantial recovery could potentially qualify if genuinely conducted for environmental assessment.

24. **§ 3(c)—Mixed-purpose activities are unresolved.** The text does not require environmental assessment to be the sole or primary purpose. It therefore leaves uncertain whether an operation serving both assessment and commercial objectives is exempt.

25. **§ 3(c)—No approval or substantiation process.** The bill requires no advance authorization, independent research protocol, certification, or publication of findings to invoke the exception. This creates an enforcement dispute over purpose rather than a clear ex ante boundary.

### Registration and reporting

26. **§§ 2(3), 4—Registry coverage does not match prohibited activity.** Vessels of exactly 5,000 gross tons or less fall outside the registry even if they conduct prohibited mining. Conversely, larger equipped vessels must apparently register even if idle or conducting exempt activity; registration is not permission to mine.

27. **§ 2(3)—“Equipped” and gross-tonnage standards are unspecified.** The bill does not address temporary equipment, modular systems, remote collection machinery, or which gross-tonnage measurement convention governs. These uncertainties affect registry coverage.

28. **§ 4(a)—No jurisdictional limitation for registration.** “Each covered vessel” is not limited by flag, ownership, operator nationality, or location. Read literally, it reaches foreign vessels operating abroad, raising practical enforcement and extraterritorial-interpretation questions.

29. **§ 4—No registration deadline or reporting specifications.** The bill does not define “operator,” allocate responsibility among multiple operators, or specify registration timing, quarterly due dates, required data, or record retention. A requirement merely to “describe” recovery activities may not produce information sufficient to enforce the thresholds.

30. **§§ 4(b), 5—Unregistered operators and registry violations are poorly addressed.** Reporting applies to “each registered operator,” leaving an awkward gap for operators that fail to register. Section 5 penalizes only § 3 violations, not registration or reporting failures; other laws may address false statements, but this bill supplies no express § 4 penalty.

### Enforcement and effective date

31. **§§ 3–5—Enforcement responsibility and procedure are unspecified.** NOAA receives registrations, but the bill does not identify who assesses civil penalties or provide inspection, administrative hearing, collection, or express injunctive procedures. Existing governmental authority may fill some gaps, but the enforcement framework is incomplete.

32. **§ 5(a)—Daily penalty aggregation is unclear.** The text does not specify whether separate vessels, sites, or acts generate separate million-dollar daily maximums. It also leaves uncertain how to count violation days for intermittent activity or an annual recovery threshold.

33. **§ 5(b)—Willfulness interacts awkwardly with discretionary classification.** Criminal liability requires willfulness, but the catchall depends on an unspecified official’s risk determination. Unclear or unpublished classifications could complicate proof and fair-notice requirements.

34. **§§ 5(a), 8—Enactment-date penalties conflict with delayed effectiveness.** Section 5(a) references violations occurring on or after enactment, while the Act takes effect 180 days later. The stronger reading is that no § 3 violation exists before effectiveness, but the mismatch invites disputes over attempted retroactive application.

35. **§§ 3(b), 8—The grandfathering cutoff precedes effectiveness.** Licenses issued during the 180-day interval are not grandfathered, even though the prohibition is not yet effective. The bill leaves transition treatment of ongoing operations and annual tonnage accounting unresolved.

### International agreement and duration

36. **§ 6—The negotiation deadline has an uncertain deliverable.** “Shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months” could refer to beginning efforts or seeking completion by that date. It does not require a concluded agreement or provide a fallback if negotiations fail.

37. **§ 6—“Equivalent” international prohibitions are undefined.** It is unclear whether equivalence requires the domestic exceptions, person-based jurisdiction, risk catchall, or sunset. The provision also does not itself prohibit foreign operations or supply implementing authority for an eventual agreement.

38. **§ 7(a)—The prerequisite National Academies report is not commissioned.** No provision directs preparation of the report, sets a deadline, supplies funding, or defines its scope. The early-termination mechanism could therefore lack the report it requires.

39. **§ 7(a)—“Without serious harm” lacks an assessment standard.** The text specifies no affected ecosystems, spatial or temporal scale, acceptable uncertainty, or meaning of “serious.” It also does not explain whether Congress may make a finding for particular technologies or locations rather than commercial mining generally.

40. **§ 7(a)—Early termination leaves other provisions apparently intact.** The joint-resolution mechanism ends the § 3 prohibition, not expressly the registry, reporting duties, or rest of the Act. This creates a potentially burdensome residual regime after mining becomes permissible.

41. **§§ 7(a), 7(b)—The sunset overrides the scientific-condition mechanism.** The entire Act expires after ten years even without a favorable report or congressional finding. Thus, the prohibition is not necessarily maintained until mining can occur “without serious harm.”

42. **§§ 7(b), 8—The operative period is shorter than ten years.** Sunset runs from enactment, while effectiveness begins 180 days later. The prohibition therefore operates for approximately nine and a half years, not ten.

43. **§ 7(b)—No express transition or savings provisions.** The bill does not address pending enforcement, existing reporting obligations, or records at sunset. The general federal saving statute may preserve accrued liabilities, so expiration should not be treated as automatically erasing prior violations.
